Seer: Guiding Small Deep-Research Agents with Shared Decision Models

Yuhao Zhou Affiliation: Sichuan University    Yang Zhou Affiliation: Sichuan University    Yuanxi Li Affiliation: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign    Jindi Lv Affiliation: Sichuan University    Dan Si Affiliation: Lenovo Group Limited    Qing Ye Affiliation: Sichuan University    Jiancheng Lv ††thanks: Corresponding author: Jiancheng Lv. Affiliation: Sichuan University
Abstract

Deep-research agents repeatedly decide what to search, read, and verify, often using large cloud-hosted language models for action proposal. However, privacy and local control motivate running agents on users’ devices, where limited memory and compute favor smaller models and complicate on-device training. Yet inference-time guidance faces three obstacles: exploring alternatives through real execution adds tool calls, prompted self-evaluation is bounded by the agent’s judgment, and model-specific guidance risks repeated adaptation costs. We introduce Seer, an inference-time framework providing local guidance that separates the agent’s action proposal from learned consequence prediction and value estimation. From a shared corpus of real research trajectories, we train two models: a tool-response simulator on observed call–response pairs and a value estimator on histories labeled with discounted terminal correctness. The simulator and estimator are trained offline and reused across agents without further training. Moreover, Seer executes only the selected action and adds only real tool responses to the committed history, avoiding tool calls on discarded candidates at additional inference cost. Across multiple deep-research benchmarks, Seer substantially improves agent performance for different language models. For instance, GAIA accuracy rises from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and from 22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Furthermore, our analyses suggest that broader candidate coverage can compensate for imperfect simulation, while prediction and scoring errors limit the benefits of wider imagined search. These findings highlight the potential of reusable models for prediction and evaluation to strengthen small research agents through extra local computation without the real execution of the discarded candidates.

1 Introduction

Deep-research agents use language models to decide what to search, read, and verify, integrating evidence across sources to answer complex questions [64]. In practice, OpenAI Deep Research [43] and Gemini Deep Research [11] offer multi-step web investigation and source-linked reports, while open efforts such as DeepResearcher [65] and Tongyi DeepResearch [53] advance research on sustained information seeking. Meanwhile, benchmarks from GAIA’s real-world reasoning and tool-use questions [39] to BrowseComp’s challenging web information-seeking tasks [58] evaluate agents’ ability to gather and integrate evidence.

For users applying these capabilities to sensitive tasks, keeping an agent’s reasoning and decision-making on-device offers greater local control, a motivation reflected in privacy-oriented personal assistants [2]. However, deploying these agents on users’ devices requires managing both local computational resources and external tool-use costs. Memory and compute constraints favor smaller language models [4], while tool-call fees make repeated searches and page retrievals an additional deployment expense [34].

Under these constraints, training small models specifically for research is a natural way to improve agent performance. However, collecting training data and optimizing each model require additional resources, making repeated adaptation costly for resource-constrained deployments. Instead, inference-time methods offer an alternative by improving agent decisions without updating the deployed model. Specifically, output-level refinement [57, 63, 56] selects or revises completed answers but cannot redirect actions already executed. Decision-level evaluation [66, 28, 59, 60] guides intermediate choices through search or learned critics, but evaluating branches through real execution incurs tool costs even for discarded candidates. Model-based lookahead [24, 20, 5] reduces this overhead by evaluating predicted consequences before execution. To avoid shifting adaptation costs to supporting components, such guidance should transfer across agent models without retraining. Yet approaches relying on the agent’s model for prompted prediction and scoring remain bounded by its capabilities [55]. Figure 1 summarizes these limitations. The challenge is therefore to provide reusable guidance that strengthens small agents without model-specific retraining or the real execution of discarded candidates.

We introduce Seer, an inference-time framework providing local guidance in deep research. Our key idea is to decouple action proposal from tool-response prediction and value estimation to enable reusable guidance across agents. From a shared corpus of real research trajectories collected across tasks and agents, we train two models: a tool-response simulator on observed call–response pairs and a value estimator on interaction histories labeled with discounted terminal correctness. These complementary supervision signals teach the simulator to predict what an action may reveal and the estimator to assess how the resulting history relates to eventual task success. The simulator and estimator are trained offline and shared across agents powered by different models. Deployment requires neither updating the agent’s model nor retraining the simulator or estimator. Specifically, at inference, the agent proposes candidate actions, the simulator predicts their tool responses, and the estimator scores the resulting imagined histories to guide action selection. Seer executes only the selected action and adds real tool responses to the committed history. Candidate evaluation therefore uses additional inference computation rather than real tool calls on discarded alternatives, while the agent retains real rather than simulated responses as evidence. Our contributions are threefold.

  1. 1.

    We propose Seer, an inference-time framework that decouples action proposal from shared tool-response prediction and history-level value estimation across agents. This design enables reusable guidance for frozen agents without any model-specific retraining or the real execution of the discarded candidates.

  2. 2.

    We develop a shared training pipeline that collects real trajectories across agents and tasks through Monte Carlo branching on existing datasets. The resulting large-scale training corpus provides complementary supervision: observed call–response pairs for the simulator and history prefixes labeled with discounted terminal correctness for the value estimator.

  3. 3.

    Experiments with different models across extensive benchmarks demonstrate substantial gains for small agents, with benefits extending to larger-model settings. Ablations and analyses reveal the trade-off between candidate coverage and imperfect prediction and scoring.

2 Related Work

Research agents and tool use. Research agents couple a language model’s parametric knowledge with information acquired through tools: WebGPT [41] combines browser-assisted question answering with human feedback, ReAct [62] interleaves reasoning with actions, and Toolformer [48] learns when to invoke APIs from self-supervised examples. Within this setting, the task determines which observations matter: an agent must judge which query or goal-conditioned page visit is likely to reveal useful evidence, which creates two deployment costs—the local compute to run the model and the external tool calls to gather evidence. Quantization [33], context management [55], and tool budgeting [34] address deployment costs, while compact research agents [6, 30, 54] target research capability. Distillation [21, 1] and reinforcement learning [27, 65] strengthen the agent’s model but require optimization for each adapted model. Seer instead trains reusable decision models, complementing these efficiency-oriented approaches without updating or retraining the deployed agent.

Inference-time guidance. Guidance can act on completed outputs or intervene at intermediate decisions, and the distinction matters because producing a candidate answer may already consume substantial tool calls. Output-level methods select or revise solutions: self-consistency [57] aggregates independently sampled reasoning paths, Self-Refine [38] alternates generation with feedback, and learned verifiers [12] score candidates, with asymmetric verification [63] allocating a modest verification budget to select among expensive search trajectories. These methods cannot recover tool calls already spent on discarded trajectories, as our BoN@4 and AV@4 baselines illustrate. Decision-level methods intervene earlier: Tree of Thoughts [61] explores intermediate reasoning states with self-evaluation, Reflexion [50] uses verbal feedback from earlier attempts, LATS [66] and web-agent tree search [28] combine search with environmental feedback, and AgentRM [59] learns a transferable reward model. Process-supervision evaluators [31, 36, 9, 60] further supply learned ranking signals, but branches explored through real interaction still incur tool calls even when discarded, and prompted self-evaluation depends on the agent’s judgment.

Model-based lookahead. A learned or prompted world model can instead predict aspects of a candidate’s outcome before execution. Dyna [52] integrates real experience with model-based planning, MuZero [49] learns latent dynamics together with planning-relevant predictions, and Dreamer-style agents [23, 26] train behavior from imagined rollouts; for language agents, DreamGym [8] and DynaWeb [14] use predicted experience to train the agent itself. At inference time, RAP [24] repurposes an LLM as a world model within tree search, while WMA [5] and WebDreamer [20] learn transition predictions for web navigation; SiRA [13] plans with natural-language belief states, and MCP-Cosmos [18] couples world models with tool interfaces. However, predicted experience in these works either trains the agent or guides a single navigation decision, and avoiding real candidate execution does not by itself ensure that both prediction and evaluation transfer across agent models without retraining. To enable this reuse, Seer separates call-level response prediction and history-level evaluation from the agent model, training the evaluator on discounted terminal correctness and reusing both checkpoints across agents. It executes only the selected action and retains real responses as evidence, trading additional local inference for candidate comparison without tool calls on discarded candidates.

3 Problem Formulation

Given a request qq, a deep-research agent 𝒢\mathcal{G} uses a language model to decide what to search, read, and verify, integrating evidence across sources to produce an answer or report a^\hat{a} [64]. During a run, the agent maintains a committed interaction history sts_{t}, which initially contains qq and the agent instructions. At round tt, it uses this history to select an action ata_{t} that either submits a final answer without tool calls or issues one or more tool calls. To describe this choice mathematically, let π𝒢(⋅∣st)\pi_{\mathcal{G}}(\cdot\mid s_{t}) denote the agent’s distribution over actions given the current history.

Let ℰ\mathcal{E} denote the real tool-execution operator, which invokes the tools specified in ata_{t} with their arguments in the current external environment and returns the responses oto_{t}. Action selection and the history update for a nonterminal interaction are then written as

at∼π𝒢(⋅∣st),ot=ℰ(at),st+1=st⊕(at,ot),a_{t}\sim\pi_{\mathcal{G}}(\cdot\mid s_{t}),\quad o_{t}=\mathcal{E}(a_{t}),\quad s_{t+1}=s_{t}\oplus(a_{t},o_{t}), (1)

where ⊕\oplus denotes concatenation. Thus, the next action is selected using a history that includes the previous history, the selected action, and its real tool responses. A final-answer submission instead terminates the run with ot=∅o_{t}=\varnothing.

We denote the full execution record by ξ\xi and assess its outcome using a task-dependent terminal quality score Rterm​(ξ,q)∈[0,1]R_{\mathrm{term}}(\xi;q)\in[0,1]. For the question-answering tasks considered here, this score is 1 for a correct final answer and 0 otherwise, including unanswered tasks. Gold answers are used only for evaluation and offline supervision, not for inference-time decisions. For requests q∼𝒟q\sim\mathcal{D} drawn from the task distribution and traces ξ\xi generated by 𝒢\mathcal{G} through real tool interactions, the objective is

max𝒢⁡𝔼q∼𝒟,ξ​[Rterm​(ξ,q)].\max_{\mathcal{G}}\;\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D},\xi}\big[R_{\mathrm{term}}(\xi;q)\big]. (2)

When the agent’s reasoning and decision-making run on-device, this objective is constrained by local model memory and the cost of real tool calls to external services. We denote the total number of locally deployed model parameters by cparamc_{\mathrm{param}} and the number of real tool calls by ctoolc_{\mathrm{tool}}, and collect them in

𝐜⁡(𝒢,ξ)=(cparam​(𝒢),ctool​(ξ))⊤.\mathbf{c}(\mathcal{G},\xi)=\big(c_{\mathrm{param}}(\mathcal{G}),\,c_{\mathrm{tool}}(\xi)\big)^{\top}. (3)

Given the corresponding budget vector 𝐁\mathbf{B}, the on-device problem becomes

max𝒢⁡𝔼q∼𝒟,ξ​[Rterm​(ξ,q)]s.t.𝐜⁡(𝒢,ξ)⪯𝐁,\max_{\mathcal{G}}\;\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D},\xi}\big[R_{\mathrm{term}}(\xi;q)\big]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathbf{c}(\mathcal{G},\xi)\preceq\mathbf{B}, (4)

where ⪯\preceq denotes componentwise inequality. The per-run count ctoolc_{\mathrm{tool}} includes all real calls recorded in ξ\xi, including those made for discarded candidates, with batched calls counted individually. A run stops on submission or when the budget is exhausted.

To compare candidates without increasing ctoolc_{\mathrm{tool}}, let ℰ^\widehat{\mathcal{E}} denote a local approximation to tool responses, following planning with predicted action outcomes [24, 20]. For a candidate action a(i)a^{(i)} at history sts_{t}, the predicted response and imagined history are

o^(i)=ℰ^​(a(i)),s^(i)=st⊕(a(i),o^(i)),\hat{o}^{(i)}=\widehat{\mathcal{E}}(a^{(i)}),\qquad\hat{s}^{(i)}=s_{t}\oplus(a^{(i)},\hat{o}^{(i)}), (5)

with o^(i)=∅\hat{o}^{(i)}=\varnothing for final-answer candidates. These imagined histories support candidate comparison, while the committed update still uses ot=ℰ⁡(at)o_{t}=\mathcal{E}(a_{t}). Our focus is therefore to improve the objective in Eq. (4) for a fixed agent model using predicted outcomes for action selection, while satisfying the same resource budgets. Appendix A summarizes the notation used throughout the paper.

4 Our Approach

The response approximation in §3 leaves two questions: what might a candidate action reveal, and how useful is the resulting history for completing the task? Seer addresses them with a tool-response simulator WϕW_{\phi} and a value estimator VθV_{\theta} supervised by observed responses and discounted terminal correctness, respectively, while the agent’s frozen model proposes actions (Figure 2). We refer to these two components jointly as the decision models, and individually as the simulator and estimator.

4.1 Decoupling Prediction from Evaluation

Predicting tool responses. Let π\pi denote the frozen agent model’s action-proposal distribution and calls⁡(a)\operatorname{calls}(a) the tool invocations in action aa. For each call cc, containing a tool name and arguments, WϕW_{\phi} generates a response o^c\hat{o}_{c} conditioned only on that call and a tool-specific instruction. Collecting these responses in call order implements the local approximation

o^c∼Wϕ(⋅∣c),ℰ^(a)=(o^c)c∈calls⁡(a).\hat{o}_{c}\sim W_{\phi}(\cdot\mid c),\qquad\widehat{\mathcal{E}}(a)=\bigl(\hat{o}_{c}\bigr)_{c\in\operatorname{calls}(a)}. (6)

This interface omits conversation history and agent identity, allowing reuse across agents with a common tool schema.

Evaluating candidate histories. Predicting a response does not establish its usefulness; VθV_{\theta} therefore evaluates the resulting history using supervision from terminal task outcomes. For each proposal a(i)∼π(⋅∣st)a^{(i)}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s_{t}), we construct the imagined history as in Eq. (5) and evaluate it with VθV_{\theta}:

s^(i)=st⊕(a(i),ℰ^​(a(i))),v(i)=Vθ​(s^(i)).\hat{s}^{(i)}=s_{t}\oplus\bigl(a^{(i)},\widehat{\mathcal{E}}(a^{(i)})\bigr),\qquad v^{(i)}=V_{\theta}(\hat{s}^{(i)}). (7)

For final-answer candidates, ℰ^​(a(i))=∅\widehat{\mathcal{E}}(a^{(i)})=\varnothing, so the estimator scores the history with the proposed answer appended. Search uses these scores to change the overall action-selection distribution π𝒢\pi_{\mathcal{G}}, not the proposal distribution π\pi. Both learned components are trained offline and reused across agents without further training.

4.2 Learning from Real Research Trajectories

We collect a shared corpus using agents powered by different frozen language models on training questions disjoint from the evaluation questions. Inspired by Monte Carlo search for process-supervision collection [36], we branch from intermediate histories to collect alternative continuations, all through real tool execution. The same trajectories thus supply two complementary signals: observed responses for WϕW_{\phi} and discounted terminal correctness for VθV_{\theta}.

Learning Tool-Response Prediction: We extract individual call–response pairs from the corpus, normalize calls, remove infrastructure failures, and deduplicate to obtain 𝒟W={(ci,oi)}i=1NW\mathcal{D}_{W}=\{(c_{i},o_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N_{W}} with NWN_{W} retained pairs. Unlike value supervision, response supervision does not depend on terminal correctness: even an unsuccessful trajectory can contain valid tool outputs.

Starting from a pretrained autoregressive language model, we optimize its trainable parameters ϕ\phi using a response-only negative log-likelihood:

ℒW(ϕ)=−𝔼(c,o)∼𝒟W∑ℓ=1|o|logWϕ(oℓ∣c,o<ℓ),\mathcal{L}_{W}(\phi)=-\mathbb{E}_{(c,o)\sim\mathcal{D}_{W}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{|o|}\log W_{\phi}(o_{\ell}\mid c,o_{<\ell}), (8)

where oℓo_{\ell} is response token ℓ\ell and o<ℓo_{<\ell} denotes its preceding tokens. The tool-specific instruction and call are omitted from the loss; training and inference use the same input template (Appendix D).

Learning Outcome-Supervised Value Estimation: For value supervision, we deduplicate trajectories with submitted answers, excluding unanswered error or timeout runs. A judge compares each submission with its gold answer to assign Rterm​(ξ,qξ)∈{0,1}R_{\mathrm{term}}(\xi;q_{\xi})\in\{0,1\}; gold answers enter only label construction, never the estimator input. For a trajectory ξ\xi with question qξq_{\xi} and terminal history index TξT_{\xi}, we label each retained prefix by discounted terminal correctness:

𝒟V={(sξ,t,Gξ,t)}ξ,t,Gξ,t=γTξ−t​Rterm​(ξ,qξ),\mathcal{D}_{V}=\{(s_{\xi,t},G_{\xi,t})\}_{\xi,t},\qquad G_{\xi,t}=\gamma^{T_{\xi}-t}R_{\mathrm{term}}(\xi;q_{\xi}), (9)

where 0<γ<10<\gamma<1 discounts remaining interaction steps, not tokens or individual tool calls. Incorrect trajectories receive zero throughout; correct ones receive increasing targets toward completion. Consequently, VθV_{\theta} ranks histories by outcome and proximity to completion rather than estimating a calibrated success probability for a deployment model.

We replace a pretrained language model’s head with an HL-Gauss classification head [16], with θ\theta denoting the resulting model’s trainable parameters. Let β0<⋯<βK\beta_{0}<\cdots<\beta_{K} delimit KK uniform bins over an interval covering the targets, with centers zb=(βb−1+βb)/2z_{b}=(\beta_{b-1}+\beta_{b})/2. For a target GG, Gaussian smoothing with standard deviation σ\sigma assigns the normalized bin masses

yb​(G)=Φ⁡((βb−G)/σ)−Φ⁡((βb−1−G)/σ)Φ⁡((βK−G)/σ)−Φ⁡((β0−G)/σ),y_{b}(G)=\frac{\Phi\!\left((\beta_{b}-G)/\sigma\right)-\Phi\!\left((\beta_{b-1}-G)/\sigma\right)}{\Phi\!\left((\beta_{K}-G)/\sigma\right)-\Phi\!\left((\beta_{0}-G)/\sigma\right)}, (10)

where Φ\Phi is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Given predicted bin probabilities pθ​(b∣s)p_{\theta}(b\mid s), we minimize soft-label cross-entropy and decode by expectation:

ℒV​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{V}(\theta) =−𝔼(s,G)∼𝒟V∑b=1Kyb(G)logpθ(b∣s),\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{(s,G)\sim\mathcal{D}_{V}}\sum_{b=1}^{K}y_{b}(G)\log p_{\theta}(b\mid s), (11)
Vθ​(s)\displaystyle V_{\theta}(s) =∑b=1Kzb​pθ​(b∣s).\displaystyle=\sum_{b=1}^{K}z_{b}p_{\theta}(b\mid s).

For efficient training, each trajectory is encoded once in a causal forward pass, with scores read at its labeled prefix endpoints. This requires token-identical shared prefixes and exclusion of trajectories beyond the context limit. Training and validation are split by question, keeping all trajectories and prefixes for the same question together.

4.3 Imagined Search and Real Execution

At each real round, Seer builds a fresh tree rooted at the committed history sts_{t} and runs NsimN_{\mathrm{sim}} simulations using predictor upper confidence bound applied to trees (PUCT) [47, 51]. Algorithm 1 in Appendix C gives the complete round, with candidate width kk and depth cap dmaxd_{\max}. Here, a search simulation is one tree traversal and value backup, distinct from predicting an individual tool response with the simulator.

Candidate expansion. At an expandable history s¯\bar{s}, we independently sample mm valid actions from π(⋅∣s¯)\pi(\cdot\mid\bar{s}), with 1≤m≤k1\leq m\leq k, and batch their tool calls through WϕW_{\phi}. The resulting imagined histories become children with uniform edge priors P⁡(e)=1/mP(e)=1/m; final-answer children are terminal. Because VθV_{\theta} is trained on real histories, simulation errors can distort its rankings, motivating the depth cap.

Selection and backup. For an edge ee with parent node uu, selection uses

score⁡(e)=Q⁡(e)+cpuct​P​(e)​N⁡(u)+11+N⁡(e),\operatorname{score}(e)=Q(e)+c_{\mathrm{puct}}P(e)\frac{\sqrt{N(u)+1}}{1+N(e)}, (12)

where N⁡(u)N(u) and N⁡(e)N(e) are visit counts, Q⁡(e)Q(e) is the mean backed-up value, and cpuctc_{\mathrm{puct}} controls exploration. Each simulation scores its endpoint with VθV_{\theta} and backs up that value along the traversed path, including when the endpoint is terminal or depth-capped. Thus, terminal candidates are evaluated by the learned estimator, not by real execution or gold-answer judgments.

Real execution. After search, we commit the action on the most-visited root edge:

e∗∈arg⁡maxe∈root​edges⁡N⁡(e),at=action⁡(e∗).e^{*}\in\arg\max_{e\in\mathrm{root\ edges}}N(e),\qquad a_{t}=\operatorname{action}(e^{*}). (13)

A final-answer submission terminates the run; otherwise, we execute ata_{t} and update st+1=st⊕(at,ℰ⁡(at))s_{t+1}=s_{t}\oplus(a_{t},\mathcal{E}(a_{t})). Imagined branches are discarded, so only real responses enter the next round’s root history. Accordingly, Seer’s real tool-call count is given by

ctool​(ξ)=∑t|calls⁡(at)|,c_{\mathrm{tool}}(\xi)=\sum_{t}\bigl|\operatorname{calls}(a_{t})\bigr|, (14)

where final-answer actions contribute zero. Discarded candidates incur local inference but no real calls. Total calls can nevertheless differ from the unassisted agent because action choices and run length change. In addition, Seer uses additional local computation and model memory for candidate comparison without relaxing the resource budgets.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Training Setup. Frozen agents collect real trajectories by sampling questions round-robin from DeepDive [35], MiroVerse [40], Nemotron RL [42], OpenSeeker [15], and REDSearcher [10], excluding evaluation questions. This yields 0.7M call–response pairs for the simulator and 1M training samples for the estimator. All methods share two external tools: search returns titles, links, and snippets, while visit retrieves pages and extracts goal-relevant evidence. Extraction in visit is performed by a shared Qwen3.5-397B-A17B service, so its cost applies equally to all compared methods. Both models are initialized from Qwen3.5-9B [45] and use LoRA [25] at a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}, with simulator/estimator ranks of 64/32 and context limits of 16k/128k tokens. The estimator learns discounted terminal correctness (γ=0.95\gamma=0.95) through a fully trainable HL-Gauss head [16] with 201 bins over [−1,1][-1,1] and a Gaussian standard deviation of 0.75 bin widths. Both checkpoints are reused unchanged across agents.

Evaluation Setup. We report final-answer accuracy on GAIA [39], BrowseComp-200 (BC-200) [58], BrowseComp-ZH (BC-ZH) [67], SEAL-0 [44], and XBench-DeepSearch (XBench-DS) [7], following each benchmark’s evaluation protocol. The main comparison covers Qwen3.5-4B/9B/35B-A3B [45], Qwen3.6-35B-A3B [46], and Gemma-4-e2b-it/e4b-it [19]. For each model, all methods share the frozen agent and tools and use the model’s recommended sampling settings. Base Agent runs one ReAct-style trajectory [62], whereas BoN@4 and AV@4 run four and select by normalized-answer majority voting [57] and prompted outcome verification [63], respectively, without gold-answer access. We also implement RAP@4 [24], but omit it from the main table after prompted simulation and self-evaluation yield little benefit on 4B/9B agents, as illustrated in Table 1. Each trajectory is limited to 100 committed agent rounds, 128k input tokens, and 9000 s, with a direct-answer attempt upon reaching a limit. Speculative proposals do not count toward the round limit. Seer uses depth-one imagined search with candidate width k∈{4,8,16,32}k\in\{4,8,16,32\}, reporting k=4k=4 and k=32k=32 as low-width and scaled settings in the main comparison. These widths are not compute-matched to four full trajectories, whose real tool calls are all incurred, while Seer executes only selected actions. In tables, Base, BoN, and AV abbreviate Base Agent, BoN@4, and AV@4, respectively; SkS_{k} denotes Seer with candidate width kk, labeled Seer@kk in figures. In all result tables, bold and underlined values indicate the best and second-best results within each comparison group, respectively, including ties.

5.2 Analysis

Main Results Across Agent Models: Table 2 shows that Seer supports Qwen and Gemma agents, reusing the same simulator and estimator without model-specific retraining. With four candidates per decision (S4S_{4}), Seer outperforms both four-trajectory baselines on all five benchmarks with Qwen3.5-4B and reaches 47.0% on XBench-DeepSearch with 9B, versus 38.0% for both baselines. Expanding to S32S_{32} raises GAIA accuracy to 41.7% and 50.5% for 4B and 9B, respectively, and surpasses both baselines on every benchmark with 9B. Gains extend to Gemma-4, with S32S_{32} raising GAIA accuracy from 20.4% to 31.1% for e2b-it and from 21.4% to 36.9% for e4b-it. Across all six models, S32S_{32} improves over Base Agent in 26 of 30 comparisons and reaches 79.6% on GAIA with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B without retraining either shared component. Unlike trajectory-level selection, both Seer settings evaluate alternatives without real tool calls for discarded candidates, trading extra inference computation for broader search rather than paying to execute every alternative.

Scaling to Larger Agent Models: Although designed for small agents, Seer also benefits substantially larger models (Table 3). Reusing the same simulator and estimator without retraining, S32S_{32} improves over Base Agent on all five benchmarks for both Qwen3.5-122B-A10B and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and outperforms both four-trajectory baselines in nine of ten comparisons. For 397B, it raises BrowseComp-200 accuracy from 34.5% to 42.5% and SEAL-0 from 31.5% to 40.5%. These gains show that Seer’s shared guidance transfers across model scales rather than benefiting only small agents, without implying these larger models are suitable for on-device deployment.

Contributions of Prediction and Evaluation: Table 4 cumulatively builds Seer from the frozen Base Agent with four candidates per decision, all executed and ranked by prompted scoring. Replacing prompted scoring with the estimator improves accuracy by 0.9–22.3 points on seven of eight models, except Qwen3.5-397B-A17B. Retaining the estimator and adding simulator predictions lowers accuracy on six models at k=4k=4 but eliminates real calls for discarded candidates. Increasing Seer to k=32k=32 matches or exceeds real-response selection at k=4k=4 on six of eight models (Tables 2, 3, and 4), showing that broader search can compensate for prediction-related losses through additional inference rather than execution of discarded candidates. Direct scoring without outcome simulation trails Seer on seven of eight models with one tie, echoing WebDreamer [20]: an action’s value hinges on content invisible at decision time, such as the page behind a search result, which only simulated responses can reveal before selection.

Accuracy versus Real Tool Use: Figure 3 shows that Seer improves the accuracy–tool-cost trade-off on BrowseComp-200 across all agents. Its tool-call costs remain close to those of Base Agent across the tested widths, whereas BoN@4 and AV@4 incur substantially more real calls by executing four complete trajectories. These results illustrate the benefit of evaluating alternatives through simulation and executing only selected actions: additional inference computation enables more effective search without paying the real tool costs of discarded candidates.

Scaling Candidate Width: Across all agents and benchmarks (Table 5), k=32k=32 falls below the best tested width in 14 of 40 settings, although it achieves the highest accuracy, including ties, on all five benchmarks for Qwen3.5-4B/9B. Optimal widths depend on both agent and task: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B peaks at k=16k=16 on GAIA and k=8k=8 on BrowseComp-200, whereas Gemma-4-e2b-it favors k=32k=32 and k=4k=4, respectively. Table 6 further probes ranking reliability by comparing the estimator’s action choice with that of a GPT-5.5 oracle given the ground-truth answer for this diagnostic. Agreement generally decreases with kk, though not monotonically on BC-200, consistent with greater sensitivity to estimator noise when selecting among more candidates. Together, these results suggest a trade-off between candidate coverage under simulator noise and ranking reliability under estimator noise. Wider search offers more opportunities to find useful actions despite imperfect predictions, without reducing per-call simulator noise, but also increases the risk of selecting overvalued branches, potentially compounded by such errors. This trade-off motivates selecting a specific candidate width rather than simply maximizing kk.

6 Conclusion

We presented Seer, an inference-time framework for local guidance in deep research that separates agent proposals from learned tool-response prediction and value estimation. Trained with complementary supervision from a shared trajectory corpus, its simulator and estimator guide different agent models without retraining, using imagined search but only real responses as evidence. Experiments show substantial small-agent gains and transfer across model families and scales, with tool-call costs close to those of Base Agent without search guidance in the measured comparisons. We believe Seer suggests a path toward capable, locally controlled research agents through reusable guidance rather than model-specific adaptation or costly external exploration.

Appendix B Extended Background and Related Work

We begin with the research-agent setting and its resource constraints, then expand the three directions reviewed in §2 with additional methods and details not covered in the main text. Efficient research agents address the cost and capability of the deployed model, while inference-time guidance improves how its proposals are selected. Within inference-time guidance, model-based lookahead addresses a further question: how to evaluate candidate consequences without executing every alternative. These directions are complementary, not mutually exclusive.

B.1 Research Agents and Tool Use

Research agents combine a language model’s parametric knowledge with information acquired through tools. WebGPT [41] combines browser-assisted question answering with human-feedback training, while ReAct [62] interleaves reasoning and actions so that subsequent decisions incorporate environmental observations. Toolformer [48] learns when and how to invoke APIs through self-supervised examples. Together, these approaches establish the interaction pattern underlying research agents: selecting tools, observing their outputs, and using the resulting information to guide subsequent reasoning. InternAgent-1.5 [17] extends this pattern to scientific discovery by coordinating generation, verification, and evolution across computational and empirical tasks.

Within this setting, the task determines which observations are useful. WebArena [68] evaluates functional task completion in interactive websites, whereas the benchmarks used in this study assess answers assembled through search and page retrieval (§6). Research agents must therefore decide which query or goal-conditioned page visit is likely to reveal useful information. This creates two deployment concerns: the local resources needed to run the model and the external tool calls needed to gather evidence. The following subsections consider improving the deployed model first, then guiding its decisions without updating the deployed model.

B.2 Efficient Research Agents

One approach is to reduce the cost of the deployed model or improve its capabilities through training. AWQ [33] reduces weight storage and inference costs through activation-aware quantization. MiniLLM [21] distills larger language models into smaller ones, while generalized knowledge distillation [1] uses teacher feedback on student-generated sequences to address the mismatch between training and inference. These methods make model compression and capability transfer central to efficient deployment. Beyond language models, STORM [37] reduces visual tokens while preserving spatial structure in visual state space models, whereas Ferret [70] adapts model partitioning and pipeline execution to changing memory budgets during online continual learning. Both illustrate how efficiency also depends on the representation and execution of computation, complementing methods that improve an agent’s decisions.

Reinforcement learning further targets the agent’s tool-use behavior. Search-R1 [27] trains models to interleave reasoning with retrieval using outcome-based rewards, and DeepResearcher [65] optimizes research agents through real web interactions. AgentCPM-Explore [6] extends this direction to long-horizon research with an edge-scale model. Alongside reinforcement learning, Agents-A1 [3] combines supervised fine-tuning with distillation from domain-specific teachers to strengthen long-horizon capabilities in a 35B model. Although such training can strengthen the proposal model, adapting another backbone requires additional optimization. This motivates the complementary approach considered next: guiding proposals at inference time while keeping the deployed agent frozen. Such guidance requires no retraining of the deployed agent, and reusing the same guidance components across agents avoids repeated model-specific adaptation.

Reuse across deployments is also studied in federated learning, although the objects being transferred differ. HyperFedZero [69] generates models for previously non-participating clients without client-side fine-tuning, while ForgeVLA [71] learns vision-language-action models from distributed robot experience without centralizing raw data or requiring manual language annotations. These approaches address model deployment and collaborative training across clients, whereas Seer reuses prediction and evaluation models to guide frozen agents at inference time.

B.3 Inference-Time Guidance

Inference-time guidance can act on completed outputs or intervene at intermediate decisions. This distinction matters for research agents because generating a candidate answer may already require substantial tool use.

Output-level refinement. Learned verifiers [12] score candidate solutions, self-consistency [57] aggregates independently sampled reasoning paths, and Self-Refine [38] alternates generation with feedback and revision. For deep research, asymmetric verification [63] allocates a relatively modest verification budget to selecting among expensive search trajectories, while DeepVerifier [56] uses test-time rubric-guided verification in an iterative refinement loop. These methods can select an existing answer or inform a subsequent revision, but cannot recover tool calls already spent producing the candidates. For example, the BoN@4 and AV@4 baselines used in our experiments execute all four trajectories before selecting an answer (§6). This cost motivates guidance before the next real action, rather than only after a trajectory has been completed.

Decision-level evaluation. Tree of Thoughts [61] explores intermediate reasoning states through search and self-evaluation, while Reflexion [50] uses verbal feedback from earlier attempts to guide later behavior. For interactive agents, LATS [66] combines tree search, value estimation, and reflection with environmental feedback, and Koh et al. [28] perform search in the actual web environment.

Learning reusable evaluators. Search determines which alternatives to explore, while evaluation determines which appear promising. Rather than relying only on prompted self-evaluation, a separately trained evaluator can provide this ranking signal. Step-level process supervision [31] trains evaluators from intermediate feedback, and OmegaPRM [36] automates process-supervision collection through Monte Carlo search for mathematical reasoning. AgentPRM [9] uses Monte Carlo reward targets in an actor–critic framework to train agent policies, rather than restricting guidance to inference time. AgentRM [59] learns a reward model for test-time guidance that transfers across tasks and policy models, while RAG-Gym [60] studies transferable search critics for information seeking.

These methods separate the model that proposes actions from the component that evaluates them. However, changing the evaluator does not by itself remove the cost of obtaining candidate observations. Branches explored through real interaction still incur tool calls even when discarded. This remaining cost motivates model-based lookahead, which supplies predicted observations for evaluation before execution.

B.4 Model-Based Lookahead

Model-based lookahead addresses how candidate consequences are obtained. Instead of executing every alternative, an agent can use a learned or prompted world model to predict aspects of the resulting observation or state. The distinction between using such predictions for policy learning and for inference-time planning clarifies Seer’s relationship to this literature.

Foundations of world modeling. Dyna [52] integrates real experience with model-based planning, while Ha and Schmidhuber [22] learn compact representations of environment dynamics and train a controller within a learned model. MuZero [49] learns latent dynamics together with planning-relevant reward, policy, and value predictions. DreamerV3 [23] learns behavior from imagined trajectories, and Model-Based Policy Optimization [26] uses short model-generated rollouts branched from real data to limit the effects of model bias. These approaches establish the use of internal simulation, with different choices of predictive representation and learning objective.

World models for agent training. Language-based and synthetic environments extend this idea to learning interactive policies. Dynalang [32] learns a multimodal world model that predicts future text and image representations and trains a policy from imagined rollouts. DreamGym [8] generates transitions and feedback for agent reinforcement learning, and DynaWeb [14] combines rollouts in a learned web environment with real expert trajectories. Qwen-AgentWorld [72] learns language world models across multiple agent environments and studies their use both as simulators for reinforcement learning and as a foundation for agent training. In these settings, predicted experience supports learning the agent itself.

Language world models for inference-time planning. Predictions can also guide a fixed agent without updating its policy. RAP [24] repurposes an LLM as both a reasoning agent and a world model, combining predicted transitions with Monte Carlo tree search and task-dependent rewards. For web navigation, WMA [5] learns transition-focused natural-language descriptions of changes between observations rather than reproducing full HTML states. WebDreamer [20] combines simulated action outcomes with value-based selection and trains specialized world models using synthesized interaction data. SiRA [13] uses natural-language belief states for goal-oriented simulative planning, while MCP-Cosmos [18] integrates world models with MCP tools to support planning before execution. These methods bring language-based prediction into candidate comparison rather than requiring real interaction for every alternative.

Relation to Seer. Seer combines model-based lookahead with a reusable evaluator for frozen research agents. Its simulator can be viewed as a specialized language world model that predicts tool responses from individual calls, rather than modeling the full external environment. The estimator separately scores the resulting histories using discounted terminal correctness from real continuations. These targets reflect observed outcomes and remaining interaction steps, not direct judgments of each action’s correctness. Both components are trained offline on real trajectories and reused across agents, rather than updating the agent through imagined experience. This combines call-level prediction with history-level evaluation while keeping action proposal separate. Only selected actions are executed, and only their real responses enter the next committed history. Seer therefore complements model compression and policy training while moving candidate comparison before real tool execution.

Appendix C Seer Search Algorithm

Algorithm 1 describes one round of imagined search followed by real execution, as introduced in §4.3. Search begins at the committed history and explores branches with separate imagined continuations, up to a depth cap dmaxd_{\max}. During each simulation, selection follows Eq. (12), and the estimator scores the endpoint to assess its potential for task completion. This value is then backed up along the traversed path, updating the mean value of each edge. After search, the action on the most visited edge from the root is selected for real execution according to Eq. (13).

Note that no gold-answer judgment is queried during search, including for terminal candidates. After a tool-using action is selected, its actual responses replace the predicted continuation rather than being appended to it. Thus, each subsequent round starts from a history containing only committed actions and real tool observations.

Appendix D Tool-Response Simulator Implementation Details

The simulator WϕW_{\phi} approximates the information returned by the shared tools, rather than the full state of the web. Its modeling unit is an individual call cc: a tool name together with its arguments. As in Eq. (6), predictions for a multi-call action are assembled in the original call order. This factorization makes response prediction independent of the agent architecture while preserving the format expected by the value estimator.

D.1 Supervision from Observed Tool Responses

The real trajectories collected in §4.2 provide call–response supervision for both search and visit. Search outputs contain titles, links, and snippets; visit outputs contain page content extracted for the specified retrieval goal. We normalize equivalent call representations, remove infrastructure exceptions, and deduplicate repeated call–response pairs. Empty results and inaccessible pages are represented consistently, while substantive returned content is retained. These steps reduce variation caused by the collection infrastructure without filtering examples according to whether the final answer was correct. An unsuccessful research trajectory can still supply a valid observation of what a tool returns.

The resulting simulator corpus contains 0.7M pairs, as reported in §6. Validation is separated by normalized call identity so that repeated observations of the same call do not appear on both sides of the split. This differs from the estimator’s question-disjoint split: the simulator learns a call-level conditional distribution, whereas the estimator learns to assess question-dependent histories.

D.2 Tool-Conditioned Prediction

The simulator uses the same tool-specific input templates during training and inference. The boxed templates below make the conditioning information explicit. The query, URL, and goal are supplied by the proposed tool call; the enclosing conversation and the identity of the proposing model are not additional inputs. For a page visit, conditioning on the goal lets the simulator predict a focused extraction rather than an undirected reconstruction of the page.

Training minimizes the response-only negative log-likelihood in §4.2. The instruction and call arguments supply context but do not contribute target tokens to the loss. This objective learns the conditional form and content of tool responses, rather than training the simulator to choose actions or judge whether a research question has been solved.

D.3 Configuration and Use in Search

Following §6, we initialize the simulator from Qwen3.5-9B and train it with LoRA rank 64, a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}, and a context limit of 16k tokens. Each training example must retain response tokens within this limit, so examples that leave no tokens for response supervision are excluded. After training, the same checkpoint is reused across agent models without further updates.

At inference, candidate calls are grouped for simulation, and each predicted response is attached only to its corresponding imagined branch. Proposals that submit a final answer contain no tool calls and therefore require no simulator output. These predictions support candidate comparison but do not serve as evidence. Once an action is selected, its tool calls are executed in the real environment, and only the resulting observations enter the next root history. This procedure allows comparison before execution while keeping subsequent reasoning grounded in real tool responses.

Appendix E Value Estimator Implementation Details

The estimator VθV_{\theta} complements call-level prediction by assessing a history in the context of its research question. Its supervision associates intermediate histories with observed task outcomes and their distance from completion. It provides an outcome-supervised scalar ranking signal for candidate histories, rather than predicting tool responses or generating critiques.

E.1 History-Level Targets

We retain deduplicated trajectories with submitted answers and exclude unanswered runs that end in errors or timeouts, as in §4.2. A judge compares each submitted answer with its gold answer to assign binary terminal correctness. The gold answer and judge output are used only to construct labels; neither is appended to the estimator’s input history. For a retained trajectory ξ\xi, each labeled prefix receives

Gξ,t=γTξ−t​Rterm​(ξ,qξ),γ=0.95.G_{\xi,t}=\gamma^{T_{\xi}-t}R_{\mathrm{term}}(\xi;q_{\xi}),\qquad\gamma=0.95. (15)

The distance Tξ−tT_{\xi}-t counts remaining interaction steps, not tokens or individual calls within an action. Correct trajectories have positive targets that approach one at completion, whereas incorrect submitted answers induce zero targets throughout their trajectories. Excluding unfinished runs from this training set does not change the evaluation convention that unanswered questions receive a terminal quality score of zero.

Discounting distinguishes prefixes associated with successful completion at different remaining distances without requiring manual step-by-step annotation. However, each target describes an observed continuation from the shared collection corpus; it does not assert that the immediately preceding action was individually correct. Since the corpus contains continuations from different frozen models, the learned score reflects this supervision rather than representing a calibrated success probability for a particular deployment policy. These semantics are preserved when the estimator ranks imagined histories at inference.

E.2 Gaussian-Smoothed Value Classification

We replace the language-modeling head with a fully trainable HL-Gauss classification head [16]. As specified in §6, the head has K=201K=201 uniform bins over [−1,1][-1,1]. Their width is βb−βb−1=2/201\beta_{b}-\beta_{b-1}=2/201, and the smoothing standard deviation is σ=0.75​(2/201)\sigma=0.75(2/201). Although the supervision targets lie in [0,1][0,1], the classification support is the wider interval [−1,1][-1,1]; the support should not be confused with the range of observed labels.

For each target, Eq. (10) integrates a Gaussian over the bins and normalizes its mass over the bounded support. This gives neighboring bins similar supervision for nearby target values, rather than treating two targets on opposite sides of a bin boundary as unrelated classes. Training minimizes soft-label cross-entropy, and inference returns the expectation of bin centers under the predicted distribution, as in §4.2. The scalar expectation is the value used for search and backup; no text-generation prompt or gold-answer comparison is required to obtain it.

E.3 Causal Prefix Training and Shared Deployment

The estimator corpus contains 1M training samples derived from the real trajectories (§6). We split training and validation by question, keeping every trajectory and labeled prefix for the same question together. This prevents closely related continuations from leaking across the split. Each trajectory is processed in one causal forward pass, with supervision read at the endpoints of its labeled prefixes. An endpoint representation can attend only to its own history, so later actions and the final submission are unavailable when scoring an earlier prefix.

Shared-prefix training requires each shorter history to have exactly the same tokens as the corresponding prefix of the full trajectory. We exclude trajectories beyond the context limit rather than changing the evidence available to earlier prefixes through truncation. These conditions preserve the intended history–target pairing while avoiding the repeated encoding of shared context.

The estimator is initialized from Qwen3.5-9B and uses LoRA rank 32, a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}, and a 128k-token context limit, together with the fully trainable classification head. Its checkpoint is reused unchanged across agents. At deployment, it scores the history formed by appending a candidate action and its predicted responses; final-answer candidates are scored with an empty response. The experiments use depth-one imagined search, so each candidate extends a real root by only one imagined action before evaluation.

Appendix F Simulator Case Studies: Predicted and Real Tool Responses

We compare predictions from the tool-response simulator WϕW_{\phi} with the corresponding real tool responses. Unlike the trajectory comparisons in Appendix G, these cases examine the content supplied to the value estimator, not final-answer accuracy or realized tool savings. The shared interface has two tools: search returns result lists, and visit retrieves pages and extracts goal-relevant content (§6). Page reading is therefore covered by visit, not a separate read tool, for which no examples are available here.

The boxes distinguish call arguments, predicted responses, and real responses. Queries and outputs are condensed where indicated, and descriptive summaries are not verbatim tool logs. Any research context is provided for the reader: WϕW_{\phi} receives only the call and its tool-specific instruction, not the enclosing conversation (Appendix D). We examine agreement and discrepancies in response content rather than treating textual similarity as a measure of factual correctness. These comparisons provide a qualitative analysis rather than an estimate of average prediction accuracy.

Appendix H Limitations and Future Work

Seer’s scope is cost reduction on the tool-call axis, not context management: it reduces how often external services must be called, while the interaction histories it reads still grow with every round. This section reports the limitations that follow from the design and evaluation choices, states why the current work does not cover each of them, and outlines the corresponding follow-up studies, grouped into five directions: the relation to context compression, model coverage, the question-answering focus, fixed search computation, and deployment cost accounting.

Relation to context compression. Seer is not a context-management method and does not compete with context compression or summarization. The two operate on different cost axes: context compression [55] shrinks what the model reads, whereas Seer reduces how often external services must be called. Seer keeps full committed histories by design, because the estimator is trained on complete real histories and retaining real responses is what preserves the separation between predicted content and citable evidence. For the same reason, we did not include a context-compression or summarization baseline in this work: such a method changes the input distribution that the frozen agent sees, so a controlled comparison would require either retraining the agent for compressed histories or verifying that a compression module preserves decision quality on every benchmark, either of which is a study on its own. Combining Seer with context compression on the same tool interface is a natural direction, as the two would reduce both cost axes at once.

Model coverage. Our evaluation covers Qwen and Gemma, currently among the most widely used open-source model families, with both decision models initialized from Qwen3.5-9B. The restriction is deliberate rather than incidental: both decision models are trained once on real trajectories and then shared by every evaluated agent, so extending the study to an independent family such as DeepSeek or GLM means collecting new training trajectories and retraining both decision models on that family, a training-scale effort that would break the controlled setup in which every agent is guided by the same decision models. The Gemma agents already provide first evidence that the guidance itself transfers across families; whether the shared 9B decision models become a bottleneck for stronger agents, and whether the gains persist when the agent is stronger than the models guiding it, are left to future work.

From question answering to research reports. We focus on question answering because terminal correctness provides a clear, verifiable training signal and a consistent basis for comparing agents. Correctness alone does not capture the quality of a full research report, where coverage, citation support, and synthesis also matter. We did not evaluate report-style tasks in this work because their supervision requires rubrics whose construction is itself an open measurement problem; adopting one would tie both the estimator’s training signal and the evaluation to a contested metric. Extending Seer with rubric-based supervision would preserve the separation between proposal, prediction, and evaluation while broadening what the estimator learns to assess.

Search depth and adaptive allocation of computation. We use fixed candidate widths and a search depth of one to compare the effect of candidate coverage under a common search procedure; deeper search couples width and depth effects and would confound this comparison. This controlled setting leaves open how much computation each decision needs, and the estimator’s discount factor is likewise fixed at γ=0.95\gamma=0.95 throughout, with its sensitivity left uncharacterized. We did not run an adaptive-computation study because such a policy must commit its budget before observing the outcome, which requires a calibrated uncertainty signal that the current estimator does not provide. Future work could vary candidate width and simulation effort according to decision uncertainty and the remaining budget, building on adaptive agent scaling [29, 34]. The aim would be to spend more computation where additional candidates are useful and less where they add little, evaluated under the same resource constraints as the fixed settings studied here.

Deployment cost accounting on local devices. By accounting for model parameters and real tool calls separately, we study the cost of guidance without tying the comparison to a particular device. These measures do not, however, establish peak memory use, energy consumption, or latency on actual hardware. We did not take hardware measurements, because they depend on a specific device profile, and single-device numbers would not transfer across the heterogeneous edge devices this work targets. We instead report a device-independent analytical estimate: each decision proposes kk candidates and runs the simulator and estimator once per candidate, so local inference time scales roughly with kk. Quantizing the agent and both decision models, sharing representations between prediction and evaluation, and tailoring batching to the device could reduce the added local cost. Evaluating these changes on a fixed device profile would show whether the savings preserve decision quality and translate into practical deployment benefits. This design exchanges local computation for performance without agent-side training, and the two decision models share the same 9B base weights with separate LoRA adapters, so the added memory is dominated by the shared base rather than by the adapters.

Progress along these directions could make reusable guidance practical for a wider range of research tasks and devices, accelerating access to research assistance while preserving users’ control over their agents’ reasoning and decisions.
